items.followUp: Differentiate between atomic mass and molecular mass.

rubric.why: Identifies the substance for which molecular mass is used.
rubric.description: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses in a molecule.

rubric.why: Identifies the substance for which formula mass is used, particularly for ionic compounds.
rubric.description: Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of the atoms shown in a formula unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining formula mass using the atoms in a formula unit.

modelAnswer: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.
Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms represented in a formula unit.

items.followUp: Calculate the number of moles in 18.0 g of water (H₂O).

rubric.why: Checks the correct mass used in the calculation.
rubric.description: Identifies the given mass of carbon as 9.0 g.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly using the given mass.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated amount of carbon in moles.
rubric.description: Calculates the amount of substance using n = m/M and gives 0.75 mol.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct answer with unit.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 9.0 g, M(C) = 12.0 g mol⁻¹

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of oxygen according to shells and subshells.

rubric.why: Checks the distribution of carbon's six electrons among shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct shell configuration.

rubric.why: Checks the correct filling of carbon's subshells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct subshell configuration.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic size changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Checks the trend across a period.
rubric.description: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct across-period trend.

rubric.why: Checks the trend down a group.
rubric.description: Ionization energy generally decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
It generally decreases from top to bottom down a group.

items.followUp: State one similarity and one difference between elements in the same group and elements in the same period.

rubric.why: Checks the orientation of groups in the periodic table.
rubric.description: A group is a vertical column in the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a group as a vertical column.

rubric.why: Checks the orientation of periods in the periodic table.
rubric.description: A period is a horizontal row in the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a period as a horizontal row.

modelAnswer: A group is a vertical column in the periodic table.
A period is a horizontal row in the periodic table.

items.followUp: What are hydrogen bonds, and are they stronger or weaker than covalent bonds?

rubric.why: Checks that van der Waals forces are described as weak attractions.
rubric.description: Van der Waals forces are weak forces of attraction between particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as weak attractive forces.

rubric.why: Checks the intermolecular nature of these forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they act between molecules.

modelAnswer: Van der Waals forces are weak forces of attraction between molecules.

items.followUp: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

rubric.why: Checks the structural reason for ice's lower density.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding forms an open structure in ice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the open, hydrogen-bonded structure.

rubric.why: Checks the consequence of the structure for floating.
rubric.description: The open structure makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than water or therefore floats.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open structure in ice.
This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on water.

items.followUp: Write the equation for the vaporization of one mole of water and state its enthalpy change.

rubric.why: Checks the molar energy required for vaporization of water.
rubric.description: States that 40.7 kJ of energy is required to vaporize one mole of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct energy value and unit.

rubric.why: Checks that the equation shows liquid water changing into water vapour.
rubric.description: Writes the phase-change equation H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), with energy absorbed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct reactant and gaseous product in the equation.

modelAnswer: Energy required = 40.7 kJ for 1 mol of water.
